Full text

Abstract

Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning, sometimes benefitting learning and other times making it more challenging. However, all prior studies investigating effects of talker variability have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used a novel active learning paradigm wherein 3-and 4-year old preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, but that talker variability does not predict word learning. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children do seek out variability, but that word learning outcomes are most predictived by their relative vocabulary sizes and not talker variability choices. These results inform theories on the roles of both talker variability and active learning in language learning.

Introduction

A challenge for language learners is that words sound different every time they are said, within and between talkers (Bulgarelli et al., 2021). How this talker variability influences learning remains an open question. Early research suggested that talker variability may be something to overcome, or ignore, through the process of invariance detection (e.g. Gogate & Hollich, 2010). However, more recent research suggests that learners attend to talker variability, and that it influences learning (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022 , 2023). Here, we capitalize on recent active learning paradigms, which allow participants to make choices about what and/or how to learn (e.g. Zettersten & Saffran, 2021), to ask whether preschoolers seek out talker variability during word learning, and how these choices influence learning.

Talker variability is a common feature of children's language experiences. Recent studies using daylong recordings find that infants hear common words from 5 different talkers on average, and that hearing more talkers increases acoustic variability (Bulgarelli et al., 2021). In turn, this variability influences word learning. Bulgarelli and Bergelson (2024) found that including measurements of acoustic variability (such as variability in mean pitch and duration) predicted more variance in when infants first produced words relative to just including frequency of each word. Similarly, words heard by more people were produced more frequently in at home recordings (Goldenberg et al., 2022). Taking another approach, Zhao et al. (2025) measured the number of talkers of different ages 2-year-olds interacted with using a questionnaire, and found that interacting with a larger number of mature speakers (operationalized as 5th grade or older, or adults) predicted larger vocabulary sizes. Thus, infants' experiences with talker variability shape their own word learning and use.

Besides more recent research establishing that variability is present in children's realworld input, the majority of research on talker variability has manipulated it in lab settings to study how it influences word recognition and learning. In these in-lab studies, the effects of talker variability are mixed. In some cases, talker variability benefits learning. For example, research using the Switch task (Stager & Werker, 1997) finds that 14-month-olds are only able to learn novel minimal pairs when they are taught from multiple talkers (Hoehle et al., 2020; Rost & McMurray, 2009). Similarly, talker variability helps 8-month-olds generalize newly learned words to novel talkers (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022). Further, Richtsmeier et al. (2009) found that talker variability supported preschoolers' learning to produce novel words.

In contrast, talker variability does not always support learning. For example, while talker variability benefits learning novel minimal pairs, it inhibits learning of distinct sounding words that can be learned in the absence of variability (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023). Similarly, while talker variability helped 8-month-olds generalize words to new talkers, it resulted in overextending what "counts" as an instance of a newly-learned word (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022).

In other contexts, talker variability is found to be unrelated to learning. Specifically, Sinkeviciute et al. (2019) found that talker variability did not affect novel word learning for 7-10 year olds, when tested in production or comprehension. Further, cross-situational word learning is not aided or hindered by the presence of talker variability (Crespo et al., 2024; Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021), when tested in production or comprehension (Contino et al., 2026). Taken together, effects of talker variability on word learning range from making the task more difficult (e.g. Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023), to not affecting learning (e.g. Crespo et al., 2024) to benefiting learning (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2024; e.g. Richtsmeier et al., 2009).

Recently, Tippenhauer (2026) proposed a unified account of the role of variability in word learning, proposing that there may be a desirable level of variability that interacts with both the learner, and the stage of learning (i.e. mapping words to meaning, retention, generalization).

Specifically, variability may be particularly beneficial when it highlights invariant dimensions of the stimuli, allowing the learner to attend to the features of a word that remain consistent across irrelevant variation (see also Rost & McMurray, 2009) and for generalization to novel instances (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022; Houston & Jusczyk, 2000; Quam & Creel, 2021; see also Raviv et al., 2022). When the balance of relevant and irrelevant variability is not "desirable", learners may not be able to home in on what features to attend to, which may interfere with learning.

However, Tippenhauer (2026) predicts that learners' age and cognitive skills can shift whether variability is helpful or challenging for learners (see also Goldenberg & Sandhofer, 2013). For example, they suggest that learners' domain-specific knowledge about how words map to the world, which is refined as their vocabulary grows, can moderate the effect of variability. That is, learners with more breadth and/or depth of vocabulary (Hadley & Dickinson, 2020) may be better able to capitalize on variability during word learning.

Another aspect of word learning that is not discussed in the Tippenhauer (2026) framework is how word learning is evaluated. Across development, word knowledge is evaluated in different ways, spanning from receptive to expressive methods, and each of these outcome measures could reveal different effects of variability. Specifically, comprehension seems to precede and/or outperform production, across development (Gershkoff-Stowe & Hahn, 2013). Hu et al. (2025) suggest that this asymmetry may be related to the more difficult task of producing a ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING word -which requires selecting a particular sequence of sounds to produce -relative to choosing the correct reference out of a series of options -which significantly constrains the number of choices. Across the lifespan however, talker variability appears to benefit production of novel words specifically, as preschoolers and adults learning novel or foreign language words from multiple talkers outperformed those who heard less variability (Barcroft & Sommers, 2005; Richtsmeier et al., 2009; Sinkeviciute et al., 2019 with adults; though see Contino et al., 2026; and Sinkeviciute et al., 2019 with 7-10 year olds). In contrast, the effects of talker variability on comprehension (and generalization) may be more likely to vary across the lifespan (see e.g. Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023; Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021; Houston & Jusczyk, 2000; Rost & McMurray, 2009) However, all of these prior studies investigating the effects of talker variability have assigned participants to predetermined variability conditions. A separate line of research argues that children are active, motivated learners who structure their own learning through attention, active interventions on their environment (Raz & Saxe, 2020), and goal directed search for information (Saylor & Ganea, 2018). For example, young children explore unfamiliar objects to reduce uncertainty (Sim & Xu, 2017), elicit labels from adults (e.g. Lucca & Wilbourn, 2018) and actively seek out information they want to attend to (such as overheard speech; Foushee et al. (2021)). In experimental settings, preschoolers and adults seek out information that reduces ambiguity about what words mean (Zettersten & Saffran, 2021). Some of this prior research also finds that active information seeking can lead to a "boost" in learning, such that children retain information better that they selected to learn themselves (De Simone & Ruggeri, 2022), though these effects in early childhood are mixed (see Ackermann et al., 2020; Bazhydai et al., 2026).

Most of this active learning research has asked what children choose to learn about (Ackermann et al., 2020; e.g. Zettersten & Saffran, 2021). More recent research has shifted to other types of sampling behaviors. For example, Sia et al. (2025) allowed children to choose how to learn, asking whether they wanted to actively sample information or receive it passively.

In the current manuscript, we extend this active learning approach to asking whether preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers during the process of word learning.

Specifically, one proposal is that active learning is beneficial because learners will seek out information that reduces uncertainty (Kidd & Hayden, 2015). If talker variability is desirable for learning novel word-object mappings because it highlights how words remain consistent across varying speakers, then participants may seek it out to support word learning, and its effects should be consistent for participants who choose it themselves and for those who receive it.

However, an alternative is that active learning is driven by individual interest, and benefits of active learning may be due to higher task engagement for active relative to passive learners (Markant et al., 2014). In this case, participants may make talker variability choices that are more interesting for them (see also Tippenhauer, 2026), but their effects may not generalize to participants who passively receive them.

Here, we designed a novel word learning paradigm to investigate whether preschoolers choose to hear talker variability during word learning, and how these choices influence learning.

Participants in the Active condition were given the choice of who to hear novel words from; they could choose to hear each word 8 times from 1 talker, 1 time from 8 talkers, or some combination in between. Participants in the Passive condition received the exposure selected by a yoked Active participant, thus equating learning experiences across conditions but manipulating active information seeking. Participants were then tested on their learning of the novel words, both in production and comprehension. We tested 3-and 4-year-olds, an age at which prior research finds that talker variability supports learning to produce novel words (Richtsmeier et al., 2009) ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING and at which children actively seek information to reduce ambiguity about word-object mappings (Zettersten et al., under review; Zettersten & Saffran, 2021).

Using this novel paradigm, we ask three questions: RQ1: Do preschoolers seek out talker variability during word learning? RQ2: Does talker variability influence word learning, measured as both production and comprehension?

RQ3: Does actively choosing variability benefit learning differently than passively receiving it?

While talker variability can benefit learning, both in the lab and in the real world, we do not know whether preschoolers actively seek this out. RQ1 will allow insight into participants' choices during word learning. RQ2 will then test whether participants' talker variability choices support their learning. Prior research suggests that talker variability may be particularly beneficial for preschoolers learning to produce novel words (Richtsmeier et al., 2009; though see Contino et al., 2026), and thus participants who hear more variability may exhibit better production accuracy. In contrast, the effects of talker variability on forming word-object mappings is less consistent when words are distinct (i.e. not minimal pairs) (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023), and during early childhood and preschool years (Crespo et al., 2024; Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021; Sinkeviciute et al., 2019), and thus talker variability may not influence comprehension accuracy.

RQ3 will test whether effects of talker variability differ for participants in the Active condition relative to those in the Passive condition. If active information seeking is beneficial more generally, or if participants are choosing talker variability that is optimally useful or interesting for them, then we expect a benefit for learning in the Active condition. However, it is also possible that participants choose variability that is sufficiently useful for learning, and that participants in the passive condition will be able to learn from it just as well, in which case we may not find an effect of condition (such that active and passive participants may exhibit similar learning). An interaction between talker variability and condition would suggest that talker variability differentially influences learning for participants who actively choose it relative to those who passively receive it.

Methods Participants

A total of 80 3-and-4-year-old preschool-aged children participated (mean age = 3.97 years, range = 3.12-4.99, 42 male, 37 female). According to parental report of race and ethnicity, 70 were White or Caucasian, 9 were multiracial, and 1 chose not to report; 8 identified as Hispanic, 71 identified as not Hispanic, and 1 chose not to report. Caregivers also reported on maternal education; 7 reported a high school degree, an Associates' degree, or some college, 26 reported a Bachelor's degree, 45 reported an advanced degree and 2 chose to not report.

Forty participants were assigned to the Active condition, and 40 were assigned to the Passive condition (see below), participant age (t (78)=0.08, p=.938) and sex (t (77) = -0.56, p=.574) did not differ between the Active and Passive condition. There is no prior research using the same paradigm that can be used to conduct a power analysis. In their research on talker variability and second language learning, Sinkeviciute et al. (2019) had a sample of 32 7-and 8year-olds, which was deemed sufficient based on findings from Richtsmeier et al. (2009), who had a final sample of 32 4-year-olds. Based on this, we preregistered a sample of 40 preschoolers per condition. We increase our sample slightly as our task has less well defined conditions ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING (e.g. not strictly low vs. high talker variability), increasing variability in the learning and potentially test phases.

Participants were recruited from the area surrounding a university in the North Eastern United States. Participants were eligible if they were monolingual English learners (no more than 25% exposure to a language besides English), and had no hearing or vision problems or other developmental delays. An additional 15 participants were recruited, but excluded due to language exposure (n = 1), being in speech therapy (n = 9), technical difficulties (n = 2), or ending the experiment early (n = 3). This study was approved by the University at Buffalo IRB and we obtained informed consent from participants' parents before data collection.

Stimuli

Stimuli consisted of 2 familiar objects and their corresponding labels (ball, apple), and 6 novel objects and their corresponding novel word labels. The novel objects were chosen from the Novel Object and Unusual Name (NOUN) Database (Horst & Hout, 2016), and the novel words were bysillabic and followed conventional rules of English. Each novel object was paired with a single label, which remained consistent across participants (i.e. not counterbalanced).

The auditory stimuli, consisting of recordings of the familiar item labels and the novel words, were recorded by 5 young adult female and 5 young adult male native speakers of English. Words were recorded in isolation, and 2 of the talkers (1 male and 1 female) recorded the words embedded in sentence frames to be used at test (e.g. "Can you find the toma"?). All stimuli were recorded in child-directed speech. All 10 talkers also recorded an introduction, saying "Hi, it's nice to meet you", to use in the introduction phase (see below), see

Table in labels (F1-F4, M1-M4) are included in the figure to highlight which icon corresponded to which talker. Top middle: Familiarization. Participants saw a picture of an apple (or a ball) in the center, with the talker icons surrounding it. Top right: Learning. Participants learned 6 novel word-object pairs (pink object-blicket displayed). Bottom left: Production Test. Participants saw one image on the screen, and labeled it out loud. Bottom right: Comprehension Test. Participants saw a grid with all novel words and heard one object labeled and they selected their response.

Participants completed the experiment with a research assistant in a quiet room. The expertiment was run in the browser, using a script coded in jsPsych (Leeuw, 2023) and hosted on a local JATOS (Lange et al., 2015) server. Participants were told they were going to play a game where they would learn some new words. They sat at a table facing a 2-in-1 touchscreen laptop ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING set up to function like a tablet. The experiment consisted of five phases (Introduction, Familiarization, Learning, Production Test, and Comprehension Test, see Figure 1), followed by the NIH Toolbox vocabulary test (Gershon et al., 2014) to measure their receptive vocabulary.

We first describe the procedure for the Active condition, and then highlight differences in the Passive condition.

The Introduction phase served to expose participants to all the talkers in the study, and to teach them the task. They were told they are going to meet all the people who they could learn new words from. They saw a cartoon image of a waving hand in the middle of the screen, surrounded by eight different colored icons in a circle, representing eight different talkers (see Figure 1). A yellow box appeared around each icon, one at a time in randomized order, and participants were instructed to click on the icon with the box around it. After clicking, all other icons disappeared and the talker said "Hi, it's nice to meet you." Participants repeated this until they heard all eight talkers.

During the Familiarization phase, participants saw an image of a familiar item (apple, ball) in the middle of the screen, surrounded by the same eight talker icons.

They were told they were going to practice playing the game with some words they already know. Participants were told they could choose to hear the word from anyone they wanted, and that they could choose the same person multiple times or pick different people. Each object remained on the screen until they made 8 choices. When participants clicked on one of the talker icons, all other icons disappeared and participants heard the talker label the image (e.g. apple). This process was repeated for the other familiar word (e.g., ball, order counterbalanced across participants).

Active Condition.

Introduction. Familiarization.

The Learning phase was similar to the Familiarization phase, but with the six novel objects and labels. The order of novel object presentation was randomized. Again, participants were told that they could choose to learn the new words from whoever they wanted, and to try their best to remember them. When they clicked on a talker icon, all other icons disappeared and they heard the talker they chose produce the label. Participants heard each word 8 times, before moving on to another novel word-object pair. This process was repeated for all 6 novel word-object pairs. Participants' learning was then measured with two different test phases. First, during the Production Test, participants were asked to label the objects out loud. On each trial, participants saw an object in the center of the screen, and were asked to label it. Participants first practiced with the familiar objects (apple and ball). They then saw each new object presented twice, order of the 12 production trials (6 words x 2 test trials) was randomized. Participants were encouraged to think about their answer and let the experimenter know when they were ready.

Participants could take as long as they wanted to attempt a response. Participants that did not initially respond were prompted by the experimenter, who asked if they knew what it was called and/or if they wanted to take a guess. The experimenter advanced the trial after the participant attempted a production, or said they did not know or did not want to respond.

Finally, during the Comprehension Test, participants heard a prompt that they could respond to by clicking on an object on the screen (e.g. "Where is the toma?"). First, participants practiced with the familiar items. During the comprehension test for the novel items, they saw all 6 novel objects on the screen in a grid. After the images had been on the screen for 3000ms, they heard a sentence prompting them to click on the one that matched the label they heard (i.e. "Where is the toma?"). Participants could begin to click on an image 350ms after the prompt Learning.

Test.

ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING had finished playing, ensuring that they did not make a choice before hearing the full prompt, but otherwise had unlimited time to respond. The next trial did not start until after participants clicked on an image from the previous trial. Each novel object was tested twice (n=12 trials), in a randomized order, once by a novel male and once by a novel female talker. Participants did not receive feedback.

Participants in the Passive condition completed the same phases. However, during the Familiarization and Learning phases, Passive participants were assigned to the order of choices made by an Active participant. During these phases, they saw each of the two familiar (Familiarization) and six novel objects (Learning) surrounded by the eight talker icons, but instead of choosing which talker icon to hear from, the talker icon chosen by their yoked Active participant was highlighted with a yellow box, and they were instructed to click on that icon to hear the word. Thus, Passive participants engaged in the same motor actions as their yoked active participant. All other phases of the experiment were identical to the Active condition.

Participants also completed the NIH Toolbox Picture Vocabulary Test (PVT) on an iPad, where they saw four images on the screen and had to click on the one that corresponded with the label they heard. This adaptive vocabulary assessment takes approximately 3-5 minutes to complete. We use the age-normed scores as a measure of vocabulary, such that higher scores represent larger receptive vocabularies for their age.

Additionally, caregivers were asked to fill out a demographic questionnaire.

Passive Condition.

Additional measures.

Data analysis

We used RStudio and R (Version 4.3.1; R Core Team, 2023) for all our analyses.

Analyses were pre-registered on OSF (https://osf.io/dtb67/overview?view_only=70e6897f5803495da28df7a1096822ef), all materials to recreate this manuscript can also be found on osf: (https://osf.io/aqpn7/?view_only=164f8cd9ee14441a805bafd0b2526879).

We calculated the number of different talkers selected for each word (ranging from 1-8), which we term TalkerNumber 1 . We also calculated the average number of talkers selected by participants throughout the experiment.

For the production test, participants could record up to 12 sound files, 2 for each novel item. Research assistants listened to each file, and used broad transcription to transcribe the attempted productions. We used a strict approach to production accuracy: participants were considered to be accurate if they produced the target word (see Sinkeviciute et al., 2019). For the comprehension test, participants responded to 12 trials, 2 for each novel item. Participants were considered to be accurate if they clicked on the target object. We calculate accuracy at the trial level (0/1) for production and comprehension. 1 We had preregistered also using a measurement of talker variability based on Shannon's entropy (an information theoretic measure of variability), but the findings with this measure are identical to those reported for TalkerNumber.

Results

Familiar items

First, we report participants' performance on the familiar trials, as that provides a baseline for their talker choices when hearing familiar labels, and their understanding of the test phases.

For the Familiarization phase, we only report data from participants in the Active condition, as participants in the Passive condition received the same choices as their yoked-Active participant.

On average, participants selected 6.61 talkers for each word (SD = 1.65), ranging from 1 talker to 8 talkers.

Participants produced the correct object label on the production test practice with familiar items 92% of the time (SD = 26%). Similarly, accuracy on the comprehension test practice with familiar items was at ceiling (M = 100%). On average, participants selected 6.10 talkers for each word (SD = 1.90). All participants selected more than one talker for at least one word, ranging from 1.33 to 8 talkers on average, see age-normed vocabulary scores. In an exploratory analysis, we investigated whether some talkers were selected more than others. Female talkers were selected more often (n = 1058) than male talkers (n = 862), possibly reflecting a bias for female talkers. We also looked at participants' first talker choice, and found that talker F4 (the orange icon in Figure 1) was selected first 22.92% of the time, almost twice as often as the others (see Supplementals). Since we did not randomize talker locations, it is hard to separate a preference for talker F4 (which could be due to their production, their location, or both) from a preference for female talkers overall.

Fifty-five of the 80 participants attempted at least 1 production, while the remainder did not attempt any productions, production attempts did not differ by condition (t (53)=0.16, p=.875).

Because of the low rate of productions, our preregistered model is underpowered to find any meaningful effects. Because of this, we report production accuracy descriptively only. Using our strict criteria for accuracy, participants' production accuracy was 3%. However, participants were accurate on 13% of the productions they attempted. We calculated an average production accuracy by participant, to test whether these are correlated with participant-level variables such as age and age-normed vocabulary scores. Production accuracy was not correlated with participant age (r=.02, 95% CI [-.21 ,.24 ], t (77)=0.15, p=.885) or vocabulary size (r=.02, 95% CI [-.21 ,.24 ], t (76)=0.15, p=.882). Production accuracy was also not correlated with average TalkerNumber (r=.00, 95% CI [-.22 ,.22], t (77)=0.00, p>.999). Production accuracy in the Active condition was 3.10%, while accuracy in the Passive condition was 3%. Turning to comprehension, participants responded correctly on 34% of trials (SD = 18%), which is significantly above chance (16%, M =0.34, 95% CI [0.33 , 0.35 ], t (959)=55.47, p<.001 ).

Accuracy was unrelated to participant age (z = -1.41, p=.159), but was significantly related to age-normed vocabulary scores (z=2.56, p=.011), such that participants with larger vocabularies were more likely to be accurate on the comprehension test.

In our preregistered model, the effects of TalkerNumber ( β=0.05, 95% CI [-0.05 , 0.14 ], z=0.98, p=.327), condition ( β=0.47, 95% CI [-0.04 , 0.99 ], z=1.79, p=.073) and the interaction ( β = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.17 , 0.02], z = -1.56, p=.119) were not significant, see Figure 3. Thus, while significantly above chance, participants' comprehension accuracy was not related to TalkerNumber or Condition. Since we found that comprehension accuracy was significantly related to vocabulary size and vocabulary scores was related to talker variability choices (for Active participants), we next add (mean-centered) age-normed vocabulary scores as a variable to our model, allowing it to interact with TalkerNumber and Condition; we note that this is an exploratory analysis we had not preregistered. The model including vocabulary size was a significantly better fit for the data than the model not including vocabulary size (p= 0.01). This model revealed a significant interaction between Condition and age-normed vocabulary scores ( β = -0.06, 95% CI [-0.12 , -0.01], z = -2.25, p=.025). This interaction suggests that while there are no differences in accuracy based on age-normed vocabulary scores for participants in the Active condition, participants with relatively larger vocabulary sizes in the Passive condition outperformed those with relatively smaller vocabulary sizes, consistent with a significant difference in the slopes across Active and Passive conditions (z = -2.07, p=.039), see Figure 4. However, none of the interactions with TalkerNumber were significant, see Table 1.

Discussion

We tested whether preschoolers chose to hear words from multiple talkers during word learning, and whether those choices had an effect on learning. We found that participants do choose to hear words from multiple talkers, hearing 6 different talkers on average (out of a possible 8), but that actively or passively received talker variability did not influence word learning. We also found that individual differences in vocabulary size predicted learning in the passive but not active condition. Taken together, this study provides novel insights into participants' word learning choices and their effects on learning, highlighting that while hearing more talkers may be the modal choice for preschoolers, it may not directly influence learning outcomes.

Research suggests that talker variability can benefit aspects of novel word learning. Here, we asked whether preschoolers therefore seek out variability when learning novel words. After being introduced to all talkers, such that participants would not choose to hear all of them out of curiosity, preschoolers chose to hear novel words from 6 talkers on average. Participants chose approximately the same number of talkers for the novel and familiar words, suggesting that preschoolers may value hearing multiple talkers, or generally find it more interesting.

Nonetheless, individual participants varied in the extent to which they chose more or less variability, with a few participants (n= 2) choosing to hear just 1-2 talkers for each word. Talker variability choices also varied by participant factors, such that participants with relatively larger age-normed vocabulary sizes selected more variability overall. Tippenhauer (2026) suggests that children must possess a specific level of knowledge about how words map to meaning to determine which features of variability could be relevant for word learning, and this may be evidenced by measuring the depth of their vocabulary. The pattern of talker variability choices evidenced here might suggest that preschoolers with relatively larger vocabulary sizes may have identified that talker variability could support word learning, and selected more talkers accordingly. At the same time, prior research suggests that talker variability may make the task more interesting (Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021; Tippenhauer, 2026), and thus participants with larger vocabularies here may have found the task less challenging and therefore sought out a more interesting experience. While not directly measured here, participants' talker variability choices could also be related to their curiosity. There are two potential types of curiosity, traitbased theories describe curiosity as a stable characteristic of having a general propensity to be driven by the desire to resolve uncertainty, and state-based curiosity which is the in-the-moment experience of wanting to know something in relation to a knowledge gap or specific uncertainty (Kashdan & Steger, 2007; see Jirout et al., 2024 for review). Both state-and trait-based curiosity are thought to be associated with information-seeking behaviors and learning, and more curious children may make choices that provide more opportunities for information gain (e.g. Jirout & Klahr, 2012). Ongoing research is investigating effects of curiosity on word learning (Caunt et al., 2026), and future research will need to determine whether participants' talker variability choices were driven by the process of word learning, baseline curiosity, or because more talkers are inherently more interesting.

We tested two components of novel word learning: production and comprehension.

Despite participants readily producing the familiar words when asked, the rate of production attempts for novel words, and production accuracy more generally, was quite low. For this reason, we were not able to model production accuracy statistically. Despite some research finding that preschool aged children produce novel words during experimental tasks (Richtsmeier et al., 2009; see Contino et al., 2026 for older children), other studies also report low production accuracy at this age (Storkel & Lee, 2011), or report needing to exclude production tests overall due to toddlers rarely producing words (Gershkoff-Stowe & Hahn, 2013). It is possible that encouraging participants to repeat words during the learning phase, as done in some prior research (Sinkeviciute et al., 2019), would increase overall production rates. In contrast to production, the comprehension task revealed successful word learning, participants were significantly above chance at learning the six novel word-object pairs. This pattern of results further highlights the asymetry in comprehension and production found in prior research (Hu et al., 2025). In the remainder of the discussion, we therefore focus on interpreting the patterns of results for the comprehension task.

Our paradigm allowed us to test whether talker variability and the ability to actively make choices about how to learn resulted in different patterns of learning. We did not find overall ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING effects of talker variability: accuracy on the comprehension task was not related to talker variability. In some ways, this suggests that talker variability selected by participants may have been sufficient for learning. In other ways, it could suggest that talker variability may be unrelated to learning for this task and age group, replicating and extending prior research using cross-situational statistical learning and word learning tasks (e.g. Crespo et al., 2024; Sinkeviciute et al., 2019) which finds that in early childhood, talker variability does not influence word-object mappings when the words are distinct from each other.

While talker variability did not predict learning, learning condition (Active vs. Passive) did. Specifically, we found that active learning interacted with age-normed receptive vocabulary size. Here, participants in the Active condition exhibited similar comprehension accuracy regardless of vocabulary size, suggesting that preschoolers in the active condition may have made choices that optimized their interest and/or learning. In contrast, participants in the Passive condition exhibited better learning if they had relatively larger vocabulary sizes. The finding that participants with larger vocabulary sizes perform better on word learning tasks is consistent with previous research documenting a positive relationship between children's receptive knowledge and novel word learning (Gray, 2004; Hadley et al., 2021). Here we extend this finding to show that preschoolers with larger vocabulary sizes are also better able to capitalize on talker variability chosen for them during word learning. This is consistent with the proposal made by Tippenhauer (2026) that learners with greater depth and breadth of vocabulary may be better able to navigate relevant and irrelevant variability.

We recently conducted a similar study with adults (masked for review). Instead of learning novel words paired with novel objects, adults were taught Lithuanian translations for common nouns (e.g. house, tree; Sinkeviciute et al. (2019)). Similar to preschoolers, adult participants chose to hear novel words from 5 talkers on average. However, for adults hearing more variability for individual words supported learning to produce and recognize these words, and participants in the passive condition outperformed those in the active condition on comprehension. These findings suggest that, despite making relatively similar talker variability choices, the effects of talker variability and active learning may change over the course of development. Previous research comparing adults and children in the same task is rare, but one study similarly found that while adults and preschoolers similarly sampled words to reduce ambiguity, these sampling strategies were only related to learning for adult and not preschoolaged participants (Zettersten & Saffran, 2021). These age-related findings are also consistent with the framework recently proposed by Tippenhauer (2026): the effects of talker variability on word learning seem to differ based on participant factors, such as age here, and vocabulary size above (see also Quam & Creel, 2021). Testing even younger participants, for whom variability is found to be useful (Rost & McMurray, 2009), would provide insight into whether choosing more variability is the default, and whether its effects change across development and/or as vocabulary knowledge increases (Quam & Creel, 2021; Tippenhauer, 2026).

Taken together, we find that while preschoolers choose to hear talker variability during word learning, their talker variability choices are not related to learning outcomes. We also found interactions between information seeking and age-normed vocabulary sizes, such that for participants in the yoked-passive condition, receptive vocabulary sizes were related to how well they were able to learn from someone elses's choices -participants with relatively larger vocabularies exhibited better word learning. This study furthers our understanding of the types of choices children make during word learning, and highlights that active information seeking interacts with participant and task factors to support learning.
